figures.caption: Figure 1. Disruption of the solid−solid interface: from solvation-buffered to mechanically constrained electrochemistry. (a) In conventional solid−liquid interfaces, the macroscopic fluidity of the electrolyte enables natural stress relaxation. (b) In solid-state batteries, the rigid solid−solid interface lacks fluidity and solvation. Thermodynamic and kinetic reconstruction from classical solid−liquid to mechanically constrained solid−solid interfaces. (c) The free energy landscape of a classical solid−liquid interface. (d) The disrupted free energy landscape at a rigid solid−solid interface. The local stresses introduce a significant mechanical overpotential (ηmech) that directly distorts the activation barrier (ΔG‡) alongside the conventional electrical overpotential (ηelec).

figures.caption: Figure 8. (a) Long-term galvanostatic cycling of a Li|LPSC|NCM811 solid-state battery. The voltage profile is coupled with particle-resolved cathode stress evolution and anode morphology evolution. Cathode particles generate GPa-level stress fluctuations, producing mechanical overpotential and capacity loss. At the anode, lithium initially deposits uniformly but progressively penetrates solid electrolyte grain boundaries. (b) Grain-boundary topology controls dendrite propagation: network-like boundaries constrain penetration, whereas Y-shaped boundaries induce stress-driven jump nucleation and accelerate short circuit. Adapted with permission from ref 1. Copyright © 2025 American Physical Society.
